extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, literary critics, and creative writers interested in heroic/poetic characterization
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating or evaluating 'hero' figures as poets/prophets in literature — what qualities a heroic-poet should show and what makes poetic language exemplary. Draws on Carlyle's lecture material about sincerity, musical thought, seriousness, and moral vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity (first and last merit in a book)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is the essential merit of a book and the foundational quality in a writer: 'the first and last merit in a book; gives rise to merits of all kinds...it alone can give rise to merit of any kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work (or a heroic figure) must feel genuinely felt and believed by its maker; insincerity is the fatal defect (the 'Simulacrum', 'Impostor'). Examples in the text: Carlyle praises the Koran for its sincerity and contrasts it with polished but false insincere men. Anti-pattern: polished, respectable falseness that utters nothing harsh and is inwardly paralysed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of vision / direct insight
rubrics_metrics.description: The author/hero must have a direct, rugged, first-hand eye for the world — 'the eye that flashes direct into the heart of things' and 'sincerity of vision; the test of a sincere heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals should show a capacity to see and state truths plainly and vividly (rugged vigor, strong wild intellect). This manifests in concrete, immediate observations (e.g., wonder at natural phenomena) rather than secondhand platitudes. Anti-pattern: secondhand borrowing and mere rhetorical flourish with no heartfelt seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as Musical Thought (musicality of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: True poetry is 'musical thought' — if a delineation is authentically musical (not merely in words but in substance), then it is poetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate/produce work for internal rhythm, cadence, and a pervasive 'melody' — not merely meter but an inward harmony of ideas and phrasing. Passionate speech naturally acquires chant-like music; the poet thinks and speaks with that melody. Anti-pattern: flat, prosaic thought even when set in verse, lacking inner harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penetration of the 'open secret' / revealing the divine idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet/prophet must penetrate and reveal the 'open secret' — the divine idea of the world or the deep, universal fact that underlies appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should aim to disclose a deeper metaphysical or moral truth which underlies ordinary appearances; the Vates (poet/prophet) makes that mystery impressively known. This is not mere allegory but an immediate, lived penetration of meaning. Scoring note: strength judged by how convincingly the work evokes that deeper reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadly earnestness and rejection of dilettantism
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic/prophetic vocation requires 'deadly earnest' commitment; dilettantism (amateur, speculative coquetting with Truth) is 'the sorest sin'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters and authors should act and write with uncompromising seriousness about the stakes; half-heartedness or playful speculation that avoids commitment weakens heroic effect. Anti-pattern: a speculative, ironical, or merely aestheticizing stance that refuses moral or existential commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitude / universality (the poet's sense of the infinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet/hero communicates an element of 'infinitude' or 'Unendlichkeit' — a feeling or reach beyond the merely particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work gives a sense of the universal or the inexhaustible in its subject; the best poets impart a quality of vastness or timelessness. Practical sign: details and images point outward to larger, unmeasured significance rather than only to themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility and depth of lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A true poet-hero is not merely a sedentary versifier but possesses capacities of action and other roles (warrior, politician, legislator) — 'the Poet who could merely sit on a chair...would never make a stanza worth much.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or judging heroic-poetic figures, favor those whose depth of perception is grounded in broad life-experience or potential for action. The poet's authority is reinforced by evidence of practical comprehension of the world, not purely literary apprenticeship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of character / freedom from cant
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic figure should appear genuine and free from cant or ostentation — candid, plain, and practicing what he preaches (Carlyle's portrait of Mahomet: frugal, mending his own shoes, not enshrined in mystery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict moral congruence between words and deeds: small human acts (frugality, tending one's own garments) can testify to authenticity. Anti-pattern: ostentatious piety, hypocrisy, or moral posturing that undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral gravity: sense of infinite stakes and duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals should convey that human actions carry 'infinite' consequence — the distinction between right and wrong is incommensurable with utilitarian calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should present duty and moral choice as absolute, not reducible to profit-and-loss. The heroic register is sustained when characters treat certain actions as eternally momentous. Anti-pattern: reducing moral action to mere utility or social calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbol/emblem to embody larger truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Coarse or concrete images (e.g., sensual Paradise and Hell) may serve as emblems for profound spiritual or moral truths — they are valid so long as they symbolize an 'everlasting truth'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic or emblematic elements that may appear crude can be effective if they point convincingly to deeper realities (e.g., Day of Judgment as emblem of duty). Beware literalizing the emblem so the symbol's representative function is lost; evaluate by how well the symbol suggests rather than only depicts the underlying truth.
